Lexis & Structure.summary: Vocabulary in context, synonyms/antonyms, correct word forms, and standard sentence structure — the main objective-test skill area.
Lexis & Structure.detailed:
"Lexis" refers to vocabulary (the words of a language and their meanings) and "structure" refers to grammar (how words correctly combine into phrases and sentences). Together, this is the single largest skill area tested in the WASSCE English objective paper, and it rewards students who read widely and pay close attention to how words are actually used in context, not just memorised word lists.

For synonym questions (choose the word closest in meaning to an underlined word), the safest approach is to first work out the meaning of the underlined word FROM THE SENTENCE ITSELF — the surrounding words almost always give strong clues — before comparing it to the options. Never pick an option just because it "sounds similar"; many wrong options are chosen specifically because they resemble the target word in spelling or sound, not meaning.

For antonym questions (choose the word opposite in meaning), remember that the opposite must be the same part of speech and fit the same context as the original word — an antonym of an adjective must be an adjective, not a noun or verb form of a related idea.

For word-form/gap-fill questions, identify what part of speech the blank needs BEFORE looking at the options: does the gap need a noun, verb, adjective or adverb to make the sentence grammatically correct? Look at what comes immediately before and after the gap (an article like "a/the" signals a noun is coming; "has been" signals an adjective or present-participle verb; a linking verb like "was" often precedes an adjective).

For spelling questions, there is no shortcut except broad reading and deliberate memorisation of commonly-confused words — WASSCE repeatedly tests the same handful of frequently-misspelt English words (like "accommodate", "necessary", "occurrence", "embarrass" and "definitely"), so building a personal list of these and reviewing it regularly pays off disproportionately.

Common mistakes: choosing an option because it is a familiar/common word rather than because it fits the specific context of the sentence; and rushing past the sentence without reading it fully before jumping to the options.

questions.question: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The politician's speech was full of platitudes.'
questions.explanation: 'Platitudes' means overused, unoriginal remarks — closest to 'clichés'.

questions.question: Choose the option opposite in meaning to: 'generous'
questions.explanation: 'Stingy' (unwilling to give) is the direct opposite of 'generous'.

questions.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'meticulous'.
questions.explanation: 'Meticulous' means showing great attention to detail — closest to 'careful'.

questions.question: Choose the correctly spelt word.
questions.explanation: 'Accommodate' has a double 'c' and a double 'm'.

questions.question: Choose the option opposite in meaning to: 'abundant'

questions.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'candid'.
questions.explanation: 'Candid' means being open and honest — closest to 'frank'.

questions.question: The committee's decision was ___ by all members present.
questions.explanation: A past-tense verb form is needed to complete 'was ___ by'.

questions.question: Choose the correctly spelt word.

questions.question: Choose the option opposite in meaning to: 'transparent'

questions.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'lucid'.
questions.explanation: 'Lucid' means expressed clearly and easy to understand.

questions.explanation: An adjective is required before 'account' (a noun).

questions.question: Choose the option opposite in meaning to: 'reluctant'
questions.explanation: 'Willing' is the opposite of 'reluctant' (unwilling).

questions.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'ambiguous'.
questions.explanation: 'Ambiguous' means open to more than one interpretation — i.e. unclear.

questions.question: Choose the correctly spelt word.
questions.explanation: 'Occurrence' has double 'c' and double 'r'.

questions.question: The results of the experiment were quite ___.
questions.explanation: An adjective describing 'results' is needed after 'were'.

questions.question: Choose the option opposite in meaning to: 'concise'
questions.explanation: 'Wordy' (using too many words) is the opposite of 'concise' (brief and clear).

questions.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'benevolent'.
questions.explanation: 'Benevolent' means well-meaning and kindly.

questions.question: Choose the correctly spelt word.
questions.explanation: 'Definitely' is often misspelt — remember it comes from 'definite', not 'definate'.

questions.explanation: An adjective is needed to modify the noun 'resistance'.

questions.question: Choose the option opposite in meaning to: 'diligent'
questions.explanation: 'Lazy' is the opposite of 'diligent' (hardworking, careful).

questions.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'timid'.
questions.explanation: 'Timid' means lacking courage or confidence — closest to 'shy'.

questions.question: Choose the correctly spelt word.
questions.explanation: 'Embarrass' has double 'r' and double 's'.

questions.question: She spoke with such ___ that everyone was convinced.
questions.explanation: A noun is needed after 'such' to complete the phrase.

questions.question: Choose the option opposite in meaning to: 'genuine'
questions.explanation: 'Fake' is the direct opposite of 'genuine' (real, authentic).

questions.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'compel'.
questions.explanation: 'Compel' means to force someone to do something.

questions.question: Choose the correctly spelt word.
questions.explanation: 'Government' contains 'govern' + 'ment' — note the 'n' before 'ment'.

questions.question: The workers demanded an immediate ___ of their wages.
questions.explanation: A noun is required as the object of 'an immediate'; 'increment' means a rise/addition.

questions.question: Choose the option opposite in meaning to: 'permanent'
questions.explanation: 'Temporary' (lasting only a short time) is the opposite of 'permanent'.

Oral English — Vowels & Consonants.summary: Recognising vowel and consonant sounds in English words, including which words share (or differ in) a particular sound.
Oral English — Vowels & Consonants.detailed:
Oral English tests how words actually SOUND when spoken aloud in Standard English (not how they are spelled), so success here depends on training your ear, not memorising spelling rules — English spelling is notoriously inconsistent with pronunciation.

Vowel sounds are grouped as: short vowels (like the /ɪ/ in 'bit', /e/ in 'bet', /ʊ/ in 'put'), long vowels (like the /i:/ in 'seat', /u:/ in 'boot', /ɑ:/ in 'car'), and diphthongs — a single syllable where the tongue glides smoothly from one vowel sound to another within the same sound, such as the /aɪ/ in 'time', /eɪ/ in 'day', /ɔɪ/ in 'boy', /aʊ/ in 'house' and /əʊ/ in 'go'. A common WASSCE question type gives four words and asks which one has a DIFFERENT vowel sound from the other three, or which one contains a diphthong.

Consonant sounds that frequently trip up Nigerian/West African candidates specifically include the two different 'th' sounds — the voiceless /θ/ in 'think/three/thing' versus the voiced /ð/ in 'this/that/then/mother' — because many first languages in the region do not distinguish between them. Other commonly tested contrasts include /ʃ/ ('sh' as in 'she') versus /s/, /tʃ/ ('ch' as in 'church') versus /ʃ/, and /dʒ/ ('j' as in 'judge').

Silent letters are another recurring focus: many common English words contain a letter that is written but never pronounced, such as the 'k' in 'knee/know', the 'w' in 'write/wrist', the 'h' in 'honest/hour', and the 'b' in 'comb/climb'. Building a personal list of these as you encounter them is one of the most efficient ways to prepare.

Exam tip: when a question asks which word is "the odd one out" for a sound, say all four options aloud in your head (or under your breath) one at a time, isolating just the sound being asked about — most mistakes come from judging by spelling instead of by sound.

questions.question: Which word has the same vowel sound as 'seat'?
questions.explanation: 'Seat' and 'beat' both use the long /i:/ sound.

questions.question: Which word contains a diphthong?
questions.explanation: 'Boy' glides from /ɔ/ to /ɪ/ — a diphthong.

questions.question: Which word has a different consonant sound from the others?
questions.explanation: 'Think' uses the voiceless /θ/, while the others use the voiced /ð/.

questions.question: Which word has the /ʃ/ sound?
questions.explanation: 'She' begins with the /ʃ/ ('sh') sound.

questions.question: Which word rhymes with 'cat'?
questions.explanation: 'Hat' shares the same /æt/ ending sound as 'cat'.

questions.question: Which word has a silent consonant?
questions.explanation: The 'k' in 'knee' is silent.

questions.question: Which word has the same vowel sound as 'boot'?
questions.explanation: 'Boot' and 'food' both use the long /u:/ sound.

questions.question: Which word contains a diphthong?
questions.explanation: 'Coin' glides from /ɔ/ to /ɪ/ — a diphthong.

questions.question: Which word has a different vowel sound from the others?
questions.explanation: 'Put' uses the short /ʊ/ sound, unlike the long /u:/ in the others.

questions.question: Which word has the /tʃ/ sound?
questions.explanation: 'Church' begins and ends with the /tʃ/ ('ch') sound.

questions.question: Which word has a silent letter?
questions.explanation: The 's' in 'island' is silent.

questions.question: Which word has the same vowel sound as 'pen'?
questions.explanation: 'Pen' and 'went' both use the short /e/ sound.

questions.question: Which word contains the /ʒ/ sound?
questions.explanation: The 's' in 'measure' is pronounced /ʒ/, as in 'vision'.

questions.question: Which word ends with a different consonant sound from the others?
questions.explanation: 'Sing' ends with the nasal /ŋ/ sound, while the others end with /t/, /d/ and /n/.

questions.question: Which word rhymes with 'light'?
questions.explanation: 'Night' shares the same /aɪt/ sound as 'light'.

questions.question: Which word has the same vowel sound as 'book'?
questions.explanation: 'Book' and 'look' both use the short /ʊ/ sound.

questions.question: Which word contains a diphthong?
questions.explanation: 'House' glides from /a/ to /ʊ/ — a diphthong.

questions.question: Which word has a silent consonant?
questions.explanation: The 'w' in 'write' is silent — it's pronounced the same as 'right' at the start.

questions.question: Which word has the /j/ sound at the start?
questions.explanation: 'Yellow' begins with the /j/ ('y') sound.

questions.question: Which word has the same vowel sound as 'car'?
questions.explanation: 'Car' and 'bar' both use the long /ɑ:/ sound.

questions.question: Which word contains a triphthong-like glide (three vowel sounds)?
questions.explanation: 'Fire' glides through /aɪə/, a complex vowel glide often described as a triphthong.

questions.question: Which word ends with a different consonant sound from the others?
questions.explanation: 'Geese' ends with the voiceless /s/ sound, while 'cheese', 'choose' and 'peas' all end with the voiced /z/ sound.

questions.question: Which word has the /w/ sound at the start?
questions.explanation: 'One' is pronounced starting with the /w/ sound, despite its spelling.

questions.question: Which word has the same vowel sound as 'day'?
questions.explanation: 'Day' and 'say' both use the diphthong /eɪ/.

questions.question: Which word has a silent letter?
questions.explanation: The 'h' in 'honest' is silent.

questions.question: Which word contains the /dʒ/ sound?
questions.explanation: 'Judge' both starts and ends with the /dʒ/ sound.

questions.question: Which word has the same vowel sound as 'blue'?
questions.explanation: 'Blue' and 'true' both use the long /u:/ sound.

questions.question: Which word rhymes with 'chair'?
questions.explanation: 'Chair' and 'care' share the same /eə/ sound.

questions.question: Which word has a different vowel sound from the others?
questions.explanation: 'Bad' uses /æ/, unlike the shared /ɜ:/ sound in 'bird', 'heard' and 'word'.

questions.question: Which word has the /ŋ/ sound?
questions.explanation: 'Song' ends with the nasal /ŋ/ sound, as in 'sing'.

Oral English — Stress & Intonation.summary: Identifying which syllable in a word carries the main stress, and whether rising or falling intonation fits a sentence type.
Oral English — Stress & Intonation.detailed:
Word stress is the syllable in a multi-syllable word that is pronounced with extra emphasis — spoken slightly louder, longer and at a higher pitch than the other syllables. Getting stress right matters because misplacing it can make an otherwise correct word hard for a listener to recognise, and WASSCE tests it directly by asking which syllable of a given word carries the main stress.

A well-known pattern is the noun/verb stress shift found in many two-syllable English words that can function as either: as a NOUN, stress falls on the FIRST syllable (e.g. RECord, PREsent, PROduce, CONtent); as a VERB, stress shifts to the SECOND syllable (e.g. reCORD, preSENT, proDUCE, conTENT). There is no single universal rule for where stress falls in longer words, so building familiarity through practice with common examination-word lists is the most reliable strategy — for instance, words ending in '-tion', '-sion', '-ic', '-ical' or '-ity' usually stress the syllable immediately before that ending (informaTION, geoGRAPHic, electricITY).

Intonation is the rise and fall of pitch across a whole phrase or sentence, and it changes the meaning or "feel" of what's being said even when the words stay the same. As a general (not absolute) pattern: yes/no questions ("Are you coming?") and polite requests tend to rise at the end; statements, commands, wh-questions ("Where are you going?") and exclamations tend to fall at the end; and a spoken list ("apples, oranges, and bananas") typically rises on each item except the final one, which falls to signal the list is complete. Tag questions ("You're coming, aren't you?") can rise (genuinely unsure) or fall (already confident, just seeking agreement), which is a subtler distinction WASSCE sometimes tests at a higher difficulty level.

Exam tip: practise saying example sentences aloud in different "moods" (as a genuine question, as a firm command, as a surprised exclamation) to feel physically how your own pitch naturally rises or falls — this builds the intuition needed to answer quickly under exam conditions.

questions.question: Which syllable is stressed in 'PHOtograph'?
questions.explanation: 'PHOtograph' is stressed on the first syllable (unlike 'phoTOgraphy').

questions.question: Which syllable is stressed in the noun 'record' (e.g. 'a record')?
questions.explanation: As a noun, 'RECord' stresses the first syllable; as a verb, 'reCORD' stresses the second.

questions.question: Rising intonation is typically used for:
questions.explanation: Yes/no questions ('Are you coming?') usually end with a rising tone.

questions.question: Which word is stressed on the second syllable?
questions.explanation: 'Begin' places stress on 'GIN', its second syllable.

questions.question: Falling intonation is typically used for:
questions.explanation: Statements and commands usually end with a falling tone.

questions.question: Which word is stressed on its first syllable?
questions.explanation: As a noun ('a present'), stress falls on the first syllable.

questions.question: Which syllable is stressed in 'imPORtant'?
questions.explanation: 'Important' places the main stress on 'POR', the second syllable.

questions.question: Which word is stressed on the second syllable?
questions.explanation: 'Consider' stresses its second syllable, 'SI'.

questions.question: A wh-question ('Where are you going?') typically ends with:
questions.explanation: Wh-questions generally end with a falling tone, unlike yes/no questions.

questions.question: Which syllable is stressed in 'eLECtricity'?
questions.explanation: 'Electricity' carries its main stress on 'TRI', the third syllable.

questions.question: Which word is stressed on the first syllable?
questions.explanation: 'Happy' is a two-syllable word stressed on the first syllable.

questions.question: In the sentence 'I SAID I'd help, not that I WOULD', stressing certain words is used to:
questions.explanation: Placing extra stress on specific words highlights contrast or emphasis in speech.

questions.question: Which syllable is stressed in 'comFORtable'?
questions.explanation: 'Comfortable' is commonly stressed on its second syllable, 'FOR'.

questions.question: A list read aloud ('apples, oranges, and bananas') typically uses:
questions.optionD: rising tone on each item except the last, which falls
questions.explanation: In a spoken list, each item before the last usually rises slightly, with a fall on the final item to show completion.

questions.question: Which word is stressed on the second syllable?
questions.explanation: 'Decide' stresses its second syllable, 'CIDE'.

questions.question: Exclamations ('What a beautiful day!') are typically spoken with:
questions.explanation: Exclamatory sentences usually end with a falling tone to express strong feeling.

questions.question: Which syllable is stressed in 'geOGraphy'?
questions.explanation: 'Geography' stresses its second syllable, 'OG'.

questions.question: Polite requests ('Could you help me, please?') most often end with:
questions.explanation: Polite requests, like yes/no questions, commonly end with a rising tone to sound softer.

questions.question: Which word is stressed on the third syllable?
questions.explanation: 'Engineer' places its stress on the final syllable, 'NEER'.

questions.question: Commands ('Close the door!') are usually spoken with:
questions.explanation: Commands generally end with a falling tone, showing firmness.

questions.question: Which syllable is stressed in 'apPEARance'?
questions.explanation: 'Appearance' stresses its second syllable, 'PEAR'.

questions.question: Alternative questions ('Do you want tea or coffee?') typically show:
questions.optionC: rising tone on the first item, falling on the last
questions.explanation: In alternative questions, the voice rises on the first option and falls on the final one.

questions.question: Which word is stressed on the first syllable?
questions.explanation: 'Yellow' is stressed on its first syllable.

questions.question: Tag questions ('You're coming, aren't you?') rise in tone when:
questions.explanation: A rising tag suggests the speaker is checking/unsure; a falling tag suggests confidence.

questions.question: Which syllable is stressed in 'ecoNOMics'?
questions.explanation: 'Economics' places its main stress on 'NOM', the third syllable.

questions.question: Which word is stressed on the second syllable?
questions.explanation: 'Agree' stresses its second syllable, 'GREE'.

questions.question: Greetings said with a friendly, welcoming tone usually use:
questions.explanation: Warm greetings ('Good morning!') are typically spoken with a falling, welcoming tone.

questions.question: Which syllable is stressed in 'matheMATics'?
questions.explanation: 'Mathematics' places stress on 'MAT', its third syllable.

questions.question: Statements expressing certainty ('That's correct.') typically end with:
questions.explanation: Confident statements generally end with a falling tone.

questions.question: Which word is stressed on the third syllable?
questions.explanation: 'Understand' places its main stress on the final syllable, 'STAND'.

Grammar — Tenses & Concord.summary: Choosing the correct tense to match time clues in a sentence, and making sure subject and verb agree in number (concord).
Grammar — Tenses & Concord.detailed:
Tense tells a listener WHEN an action happens (past, present, future) and whether it is completed, ongoing, or habitual. Choosing the correct tense in WASSCE gap-fill questions almost always depends on spotting a TIME SIGNAL word or phrase in the sentence: words like 'yesterday' or 'last week' signal simple past; 'since' + a starting point, or 'for' + a duration up to now, signal present perfect; 'by the time' + a past event signals past perfect (an action completed before another past action); and 'by [a future time]' signals future perfect (an action that will be completed before a stated future point).

Concord (also called subject-verb agreement) is the grammatical rule that a verb must match its subject in number: singular subjects take singular verb forms, and plural subjects take plural verb forms. Most mistakes happen with subjects that LOOK like they should take one form but grammatically take another:
• Collective/uncountable nouns that look plural but are singular: 'news', 'mathematics', 'physics', 'information' all take singular verbs ("The news IS shocking").
• 'Each', 'every', 'either', 'neither', 'everyone', 'everybody', 'nobody' are always singular, even when followed by a plural-looking phrase ("Each of the students WAS given a form").
• Collective nouns like 'team', 'committee', 'government', 'family' take a SINGULAR verb when acting as one unit, but can take a plural verb when emphasising the individual members acting separately.
• Nouns that look singular but are always plural, like 'police', 'people', 'cattle', take PLURAL verbs ("The police ARE investigating").
• With 'neither...nor' and 'either...or', the verb agrees with whichever subject is NEARER to it, not the first one mentioned.
• Quantities/amounts of money, distance, weight or time acting as a single unit take a singular verb ("Ten kilometres IS a long distance"), while 'the number of' is treated as singular but 'a number of' is treated as plural.

Common mistakes: assuming a compound subject joined by 'and' is always plural (usually true, but not when the two nouns together describe a single idea, like "rice and beans IS my favourite meal"); and matching the verb to the noun immediately before it rather than to the true grammatical subject of the sentence.

questions.question: By this time next year, I ___ from university.
questions.explanation: A future action completed before another future point needs the future perfect tense.

questions.question: The committee ___ its decision yesterday.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday' signals the simple past tense.

questions.question: Each of the students ___ given a form.
questions.explanation: 'Each' is singular, so it takes a singular verb even though 'students' is plural.

questions.question: The news ___ shocking.
questions.explanation: 'News' is treated as a singular noun in English, despite the -s ending.

questions.question: If I ___ you, I would apologise.
questions.explanation: The subjunctive 'were' is used for hypothetical situations, regardless of subject.

questions.question: Since 2015, she ___ in Lagos.
questions.explanation: 'Since' plus a starting point signals the present perfect tense.

questions.question: Neither the manager nor the staff ___ satisfied with the outcome.
questions.explanation: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject — 'staff' (plural) needs 'were'.

questions.question: The number of applicants ___ increasing every year.
questions.explanation: 'The number of' is treated as singular, unlike 'a number of' which is plural.

questions.question: By the time we arrived, the movie ___ already started.
questions.explanation: An action completed before another past action needs the past perfect tense.

questions.question: Water ___ at 100 degrees Celsius.
questions.explanation: General scientific facts are expressed in the simple present tense.

questions.question: Everyone ___ required to submit the form by Friday.
questions.explanation: 'Everyone' is grammatically singular and takes a singular verb.

questions.question: My brother and his friends ___ going to the match tomorrow.
questions.explanation: A compound subject joined by 'and' is plural, so it takes a plural verb.

questions.question: She ___ her homework before her mother returned.
questions.explanation: The action was completed before another past action, so the past perfect is needed.

questions.question: Ten kilometres ___ a long distance to walk.
questions.explanation: A distance/amount is treated as a single unit and takes a singular verb.

questions.question: The team ___ celebrating their victory right now.
questions.explanation: 'Team' is treated as a singular collective noun when acting as one unit.

questions.question: I ___ to the market when it started raining.
questions.explanation: An action in progress when another action happened uses the past continuous.

questions.question: Mathematics ___ my favourite subject.
questions.explanation: Subject names ending in -s like 'Mathematics' are treated as singular.

questions.question: They ___ working on the project since last month.
questions.explanation: 'Since' plus a duration signals the present perfect continuous tense.

questions.question: Either the students or the teacher ___ responsible.
questions.explanation: With 'either...or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject — 'teacher' (singular) needs 'is'.

questions.question: The police ___ investigating the matter.
questions.explanation: 'Police' is always treated as a plural noun in English.

questions.question: By next month, they ___ here for five years.
questions.explanation: A duration continuing up to a future point uses the future perfect (continuous).

questions.question: He usually ___ to work by bus.
questions.explanation: A habitual action uses the simple present tense, with -s for third person singular.

questions.question: A pair of shoes ___ missing from the store.
questions.explanation: 'A pair of' is treated as a singular unit.

questions.question: While I ___ dinner, the phone rang.
questions.explanation: An interrupted ongoing past action uses the past continuous.

questions.question: The government ___ new policies last week.
questions.explanation: 'Last week' signals the simple past tense.

questions.question: Physics ___ taught by Mr. Adeyemi this term.
questions.explanation: Subject names ending in -s like 'Physics' take a singular verb.

questions.question: If it rains tomorrow, we ___ the picnic.
questions.explanation: A first conditional (real future possibility) pairs a present tense 'if' clause with a future tense main clause.

questions.question: Both John and Mary ___ present at the meeting.
questions.explanation: 'Both...and' creates a plural subject, requiring a plural verb.

questions.question: By the end of this year, the company ___ its target.
questions.explanation: A future action expected to be complete by a stated future time uses the future perfect.

questions.question: None of the information ___ correct.
questions.explanation: 'Information' is uncountable and singular, so 'none of' here takes a singular verb.

Figures of Speech.summary: Recognising common figures of speech — simile, metaphor, personification, hyperbole, alliteration, onomatopoeia — in sample sentences.
Figures of Speech.detailed:
Figures of speech are deliberate uses of language that go beyond the literal, everyday meaning of words to create a stronger image, comparison or emotional effect — WASSCE tests your ability to correctly IDENTIFY which figure of speech a given sentence demonstrates, and to distinguish between similar-looking ones.

The two most commonly confused figures are SIMILE and METAPHOR, because both make a comparison between two unlike things. A simile makes the comparison EXPLICITLY, using the words 'like' or 'as' ("as brave as a lion", "her voice was like music"). A metaphor makes the SAME kind of comparison but states it directly, AS IF the two things were literally the same, without using 'like' or 'as' ("he is a lion in battle", "life is a journey"). If you can find the word 'like' or 'as' being used for comparison, it's a simile; if the comparison is stated flatly as a fact, it's a metaphor.

PERSONIFICATION gives human qualities, feelings or actions to something non-human — an animal, object, or abstract idea ("the wind whispered", "the stars danced", "opportunity knocked"). HYPERBOLE is a deliberate, obvious exaggeration used for emphasis or humour, not meant to be taken literally ("I've told you a million times", "this bag weighs a ton") — its opposite, UNDERSTATEMENT/LITOTES, deliberately makes something sound smaller or less important than it really is, often using a negative phrase to express a positive ("not bad" meaning 'very good').

ALLITERATION is the repetition of the same consonant SOUND at the start of several words close together ("Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers"), while ASSONANCE is the similar repetition of a VOWEL sound. ONOMATOPOEIA is a word whose pronunciation imitates the actual sound it describes ("buzz", "hiss", "crackle", "bang"). IRONY occurs when the actual outcome of a situation is the opposite of what was expected (a fire station burning down). An OXYMORON combines two normally contradictory words together for effect ("open secret", "deafening silence").

Exam tip: when a sentence gives a comparison, check first for 'like' or 'as' (→simile); if absent but a direct equation is being made (→metaphor); if a non-human thing is doing something only humans/animals can do (→personification); if a word's sound matches its meaning (→onomatopoeia); if consonant sounds repeat at word-starts (→alliteration).

questions.question: 'The wind whispered through the trees' is an example of:
questions.explanation: Giving the wind a human action ('whispered') is personification.

questions.question: 'As brave as a lion' is an example of:
questions.explanation: The comparison uses 'as', marking it as a simile.

questions.question: 'He is the black sheep of the family' is an example of:
questions.explanation: The comparison is direct, without 'like/as', so it's a metaphor.

questions.question: 'I've told you a million times' is an example of:
questions.explanation: This is an obvious exaggeration for emphasis — hyperbole.

questions.question: 'Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers' illustrates:
questions.explanation: The repeated initial 'p' sound across words is alliteration.

questions.question: In 'the buzzing bees flew by', the word 'buzzing' is an example of:
questions.explanation: 'Buzzing' imitates the actual sound bees make.

questions.question: 'The classroom was a zoo during the break' is an example of:
questions.explanation: The classroom is directly called 'a zoo' without 'like/as' — a metaphor.

questions.question: Saying 'I'm dying of hunger' when only slightly hungry is:
questions.explanation: This is exaggeration for effect, not literal truth — hyperbole.

questions.question: 'The stars danced playfully in the moonlit sky' is an example of:
questions.explanation: Stars 'dancing' gives them a human-like action — personification.

questions.question: Saying 'not bad' to mean 'very good' is an example of:
questions.explanation: Litotes uses an understated or negative phrase to express a positive meaning.

questions.question: 'Life is a journey' is an example of:
questions.explanation: This direct comparison without 'like/as' is a metaphor.

questions.question: 'The crackling fire warmed the room' — 'crackling' illustrates:
questions.explanation: 'Crackling' imitates the sound the fire makes.

questions.question: Saying 'A fire officer showing up to a fire drill late' is an example of:
questions.explanation: This is situational irony — the opposite of what's expected happens.

questions.question: 'The thunder growled in the distance' is an example of:
questions.explanation: Thunder 'growling' gives it an animal-like/human quality — personification.

questions.question: 'Busy as a bee' is an example of:
questions.explanation: The comparison uses 'as', marking it as a simile.

questions.question: 'She has a heart of stone' is an example of:
questions.explanation: Calling her heart 'stone' directly, without 'like/as', is a metaphor.

questions.question: A row of tall trees described as 'silent sentinels standing guard' is an example of:
questions.explanation: Trees given the role and awareness of a 'guard' is personification.

questions.question: 'Wilder Wanda watched wild waves' illustrates:
questions.explanation: The repeated 'w' sound at the start of several words is alliteration.

questions.question: 'This bag weighs a ton' is an example of:
questions.explanation: This is clearly an exaggeration, not a literal weight — hyperbole.

questions.question: 'The hissing snake slithered away' — 'hissing' illustrates:
questions.explanation: 'Hissing' imitates the actual sound a snake makes.

questions.question: 'Time is money' is an example of:
questions.explanation: Equating time directly with money, without 'like/as', is a metaphor.

questions.question: 'Cool as a cucumber' is an example of:
questions.explanation: The comparison uses 'as', marking it as a simile.

questions.question: Describing rain as 'nature crying' is an example of:
questions.explanation: Giving rain the human act of 'crying' is personification.

questions.question: A doctor who smokes heavily while advising patients to quit smoking demonstrates:
questions.explanation: The contradiction between the doctor's advice and action is ironic.

questions.question: 'The clock ticked loudly in the silent room' — 'ticked' illustrates:
questions.explanation: 'Ticked' imitates the actual sound a clock makes.

questions.question: 'His words cut like a knife' is an example of:
questions.explanation: The comparison uses 'like', marking it as a simile.

questions.question: 'The city never sleeps' is an example of:
questions.explanation: Giving a city the human ability to 'sleep' (or not) is personification.

questions.question: 'An open secret' is an example of a(n):
questions.explanation: An oxymoron joins two contradictory terms — 'open' and 'secret' — for effect.

questions.question: 'Sammy's silly snake slid silently' illustrates:
questions.explanation: The repeated 's' sound at the start of several words is alliteration.

Comprehension.summary: Reading a passage and answering questions on its main idea, supporting details, inference and vocabulary in context.

Summary Writing.summary: Identifying and condensing the main points of a passage into a specified word limit, in the student's own words.

Essay Writing (Narrative, Descriptive, E.summary: Planning and writing full essays in each essay type, with attention to structure, tone and coherence.

Letter Writing (Formal & Informal).summary: Correct layout and tone for formal (official/business) and informal (friendly) letters.

Report Writing.summary: Structuring a factual report with a clear title, introduction, findings and recommendations.

Speech Writing.summary: Writing a speech with an appropriate opening, body and closing for a stated audience and occasion.

Grammar — Direct & Reported Speech.summary: Converting between direct and reported (indirect) speech, including the associated tense, pronoun and time-word changes.

Registers.summary: Recognising vocabulary specific to a given field or profession (e.g. legal, medical, banking) and using it appropriately.
